_note: Finished leather goods made by the leatherworker from the tanner's leather (Complaints/612): shoes, a draught animal's harness and a sword scabbard. Every mass, hour count and life has no source found and is an estimate, marked in each yield_basis.

shoes_pair.basis: per pair of stitched leather shoes
shoes_pair.yield_basis: A pair of hand-stitched leather shoes or boots uses a bit under a kilogram of finished leather for sole, upper and thongs (no source found; conf D), cut and sewn by a leatherworker in about twelve hours (Bespoky Shoes atelier, https://bespokyshoes.com/pages/atelier, opened: 'each pair takes 10-14 hours of handwork' from one shoemaker, a modern welted shoe; was 8 hours; Round 2: Beckett Simonon, How long does it take to make a pair of shoes, https://beckettsimonon.com/blogs/resources/how-long-does-it-take-to-make-a-pair-of-shoes, opened: 'over 12 hours of skilled labor' for a welted shoe (cutting 1, preparing 1, stitching 1, sole preparation 2, lasting 3, attaching soles 2, insoles 1, finishing 1), so 12 hours agrees with two modern workshops. Leather mass, derived (Round 2): turnshoe soles are 8 oz leather (Calontir turnshoe page, https://b3r.calontir.org/events/marshal2009/shoes_1.html, opened: 'Soles were normally made of 8 oz cattle leather') and an ounce rating is 1/64 inch, about 0.4 mm (Popov Leather, https://www.popovleather.com/pages/leather-terminology-leather-weight-and-thickness, opened), so a sole is 3.2 mm; an SCA turnshoe class handout (Delftwood, https://delftwood.aethelmearc.org/medialibrary/TurnshoeClass10A.pdf, opened with pdftotext) puts the upper at 6 oz, '3/32nd of an inch', 2.4 mm. ASSUMPTIONS, labelled: foot 27 cm by 9.5 cm with a 0.75 fill gives a 190 sq cm sole; the upper of one shoe is 400 sq cm; leather density 0.9 g a cubic cm (no opened source); 30 percent of the leather is lost in cutting. Volume of the pair: 2 x 190 x 0.32 + 2 x 400 x 0.24 = 122 + 192 = 314 cu cm, 0.28 kg at 0.9, 0.40 kg with the cutting loss. The 0.8 kg used is twice that and inside 3x, so it is kept (it also covers thongs and a second sole layer); the row stays D because the clothing satisfaction below is a placeholder). Thread and nails are a few grams and are left out. CLOTHING: the pair satisfies the clothing need at the factor leather_kg already carries per kilogram of leather it holds (data/world/needs.json), so a worked pair is worth its leather and no more until a source gives cover and warmth of footwear separately; a labelled placeholder, retire with a need for footwear. Round 4 (Pass 14): every physical figure here (12 hours, 0.8 kg of leather against a derived 0.4 kg, within 3x) is sourced or derived above; the only unsourced item was the clothing satisfaction, which is a need-model placeholder (not a production figure) and stays a labelled placeholder to retire with a footwear need.

harness_set.basis: per set of leather harness for one draught animal: collar pad, traces, reins, girth and straps
harness_set.yield_basis: Straps, traces and reins for one animal run to some eight kilograms of heavy leather and a thirty-hour stitching job for a saddler (author's estimate from the size of the pieces, conf D; Round 2, opened with no weight or hours found: Small Farmer's Journal Work Horse and Mule Harness Design and Function Part 1 (https://smallfarmersjournal.com/work-horse-mule-harness-design-function-part-1/), leatherworker.net forum thread on making horse harness (a saddler there says a single 6 foot trace has 4 rows of stitching at 8 a inch, 2300 stitches, and hand-making takes 'a huge ammount of time'), and Fitz-Gerald, The Harness Makers' Illustrated Manual (Project Gutenberg 78603; leather 'from six to twenty pounds a side', no set weight); metal fittings and the wooden collar or yoke are left out). Round 3 leather area, derived: Fitz-Gerald, The Harness Makers' Illustrated Manual (Project Gutenberg 78603, https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/78603/pg78603.txt, opened) tabulates the straps of 'No. 4, single harness (hame collar)' by length and width in inches (traces 80 by 1 1/8, breeching body 44 by 1, saddle flaps 20 by 3 1/2, and so on); summing length times width over its 32 listed pieces gives 776 square inches, 0.50 square metres of single-thickness strap, about 1.8 kg at an ASSUMED 4 mm and 0.9 g a cubic cm (the shoe entry's leather density), 1.4 to 2.3 kg for 3 to 5 mm. The manual cuts light single harness from sides of 16 to 18 lb and says team and truck harness takes 'the heaviest grades', so a draught set with heavier traces, hame tugs and a breeching is perhaps twice to three times a light gig harness (ASSUMED), 4 to 6 kg, with the folds and doubled straps that the table lists as extra pieces adding more. The 8 kg used is 1.3 to 2x that and inside 3x of the derived 2 to 6 kg, so it is kept. The stitching hours have no opened source; the manual gives no hours for a set (searched for 'hours', 'days to') so conf stays D. It is a capital good of a draught animal: it is bought by whoever works the animal, so it has no household need of its own. Round 4 (Pass 14) stitching hours, rate times quantity. Rate: leatherworker.net, 'hand stitching time' thread (https://leatherworker.net/forum/topic/43307-hand-stitching-time, opened): 'Proper Hand Sewing usually runs at aprox 3 to 3.2 stitches per minute' (jimsaddler), 5 to 6 a minute for sewing alone (renegadelizard), and 'Ladies stitching for me who would average up to 30inches per hour at #8spi' (jimsaddler), 240 stitches an hour; that is 180 to 240 stitches an hour for a professional. Quantity: the forum trace in the basis above has 4 rows at 8 an inch over 72 inches, 2300 stitches; the draught set has two traces of 80 inches (Fitz-Gerald table above), stitched as that trace, 2 x 4 x 8 x 80 = 5100 stitches; the other 776 square inches of straps (0.50 m2 from the table) at an assumed average width of 1.4 inches are about 550 inches of strap, of which a third is doubled and stitched in two rows at 8 an inch (assumptions), 550 / 3 x 2 x 8 = 2900 stitches. Total about 8000 stitches, 8000 / 240 = 33 hours at the professional rate and 44 hours at 180 an hour, so the 30 hours held (with cutting and punching taking some of the margin) is within 1.5x. Kept.

scabbard_leather.basis: per leather-covered scabbard and belt for one sword or dagger
scabbard_leather.yield_basis: A leather sheath with its belt uses some four tenths of a kilogram of leather and a few hours of cutting, wetting, moulding and stitching (author's estimate, conf D). It is the soldier's kit, bought by whoever arms a soldier, and carries no household need of its own. Round 4 (Pass 14) hours, rate times quantity. Rate: leatherworker.net hand stitching thread (https://leatherworker.net/forum/topic/43307-hand-stitching-time, opened): 'up to 30inches per hour at #8spi' for a professional stitcher, 12 inches an hour for another at 8 an inch. Quantity (labelled assumptions): a sword scabbard of 70 cm = 28 inches stitched in two rows, 56 inches, and a belt of about 40 inches edge-stitched in two rows, 80 inches, 136 inches in all, which at 20 inches an hour (inside the 12 to 30) is 6.8 hours; cutting, wetting and moulding are on top. The 6 hours held is the stitching alone, within 1.3x of the derived figure; kept. Leather mass 0.4 kg: a 28 inch by 3 inch sheath and a 40 inch by 1.5 inch belt are 84 + 60 = 144 square inches = 0.093 m2 single, double for the sheath 0.12 m2; at 3.2 mm (8 oz, Popov Leather, above) and 0.9 kg/l (the shoe row's assumption) 0.12 x 0.0032 x 900 = 0.35 kg, held 0.4. Kept.
